content: 1. Report No. 15 from Alko’s Department for Economic Research and Planning, published in Helsinki, provides insights into economic and planning aspects related to alcohol consumption. 2. Saspin J, Thompson T, Stone L, and DeLand K (2003) discuss the intersection of international trade, law, and public health advocacy in the Journal of Law, Medicine & Ethics. 3. Selvanathan S and Selvanathan EA (2005) analyze the demand for alcohol, tobacco, and marijuana using international evidence, as published by Ashgate Publishing in Burlington, VT. 4. Shaffer ER, Waitzkin H, Brenner JE, and Jasso-Aguilar R (2005) explore the implications of global trade on public health in the American Journal of Public Health. 5. Shield K, Rehm M, Patra J, Sornpaisarn B, and Rehm J (2011) provide data on global and country-specific adult per capita alcohol consumption for 2008 in the journal Sucht. 6. Shield K, Rylett M, Gmel G, Gmel G Jr, Kehoe-Chan TK, and Rehm J (2013a) estimate global alcohol exposure by country, territory, and region for 2005, contributing to the comparative risk assessment for the 2010 Global Burden of Disease Study, as published in Addiction. 7. Shield K, Gmel G, Kehoe T, Dawson DA, Grant BF, and Rehm J (2013b) examine mortality and potential years of life lost due to alcohol consumption by race and sex in the United States in 2005, as reported in PLoS One. 8. Shubik M and Richard L (1980) investigate market structure and behavior in their publication. 9. Slama K (2006) provides background information for adopting policies that encourage earmarked tobacco and alcohol taxes to create health promotion foundations, as discussed in Promotion and Education. 10. Smith GS and Barss P (1991) highlight the epidemiology of unintentional injuries in developing countries, identifying it as a neglected problem in Epidemiologic Reviews. 11. Smith S (2005) addresses economic issues in alcohol taxation in the book Theory and Practice of Excise Taxation: Smoking, Drinking, Gambling, Polluting, and Driving, edited by Cnossen S and published by Oxford University Press. 12. Sornpaisarn B and Kaewmungkun C (2010) present the Thailand Annual Report on Alcohol 2010, published by the Center for Alcohol Studies in Bangkok. 13. Sornpaisarn B, Shield K, and Rehm J (2012a) discuss alcohol taxation policy in Thailand and its implications for other lowto middle-income countries in Addiction. 14. Sornpaisarn B, Shield K, and Rehm J (2012b) evaluate the effectiveness of a two-chosen-one taxation system in reducing drinking initiation and heavy alcohol consumption in lowto middle-income countries, as published in Addiction. 15. Sornpaisarn B and Kaewmungkun C (2012c) explore alcohol consumption in a traditional Buddhist middle-income country in Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research. 16. Sornpaisarn B, Shield KD, Cohen J, Schwartz R, and Rehm J (2013) conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis on the elasticity of alcohol consumption, alcohol-related harms, and drinking initiation in lowand middle-income countries, as published in the International Journal of Drug and Alcohol Research. 17. Sornpaisarn B and Kaewmungkun C (2014) analyze the politics of the alcohol taxation system in Thailand, focusing on the behaviors of three major alcohol companies from 1992 to 2012, as reported in the International Journal of Drug and Alcohol Research. 18. Sornpaisarn B, Kaewmungkun C, and Rehm J (2015a) assess patterns of alcohol taxes produced by various excise tax methods through a simulation study, as published in Alcohol and Alcoholism. 19. Sornpaisarn B, Shield KD, Cohen J, Schwartz R, and Rehm J (2015b) analyze the effect of alcohol taxation on drinking initiation among Thai adolescents and young adults in the Journal of Epidemiology and Global Health. 20. Sornpaisarn B, Shield KD, Cohen J, Schwartz R, and Rehm J (2016) investigate the association between taxation increases and changes in alcohol consumption and traffic fatalities in Thailand, as published in the Journal of Public Health. 21. Stockwell T, Auld MC, Zhao J, and Martin G (2012) examine whether minimum pricing reduces alcohol consumption, based on the experience of a Canadian province, as reported in Addiction. 22. Stockwell T, Zhao J, Martin G, Vallance K, Treno A, Ponicki W, et al. (2013) estimate the impacts of minimum alcohol prices and outlet densities on alcohol-attributable hospital admissions in British Columbia, Canada, as published in the American Journal of Public Health. 23. Sundström A and Ekström E (1962) analyze beverage consumption in Sweden, as reported by the Industrial Institute for Economic and Social Research in Stockholm. 24. Svensson J (2009) investigates travelers’ alcohol imports to Sweden at the beginning of the 21st century and whether private importers drink more or have different drinking patterns compared to non-importers, as published in Nordic Studies on Alcohol and Drugs. 25. United States Census Bureau (2005) provides data from the 2002 Economic Census, Subject Series, published in Washington, DC. 26. Vathesatogkit P, Lian TY, and Ritthiphakdee B (2013) discuss sustainable financing and governance of health promotion funds in Bangkok, as reported by the Thai Health Promotion Foundation. 27. Vihmo J (2006) examines the price elasticities of alcoholic beverages in Finland from 1995 to 2004, as published in Yhteiskuntapolitiikka. 28. Vingilis E, Lote R, and Seeley J (1998) question the compatibility of trade agreements and economic cooperatives with alcohol control policies and injury prevention in Contemporary Drug Problems. 29. Wagenaar AC, Salois MJ, and Komro KA (2009b) conduct a meta-analysis of 1003 estimates from 112 studies on the effects of beverage alcohol price and tax levels on drinking, as published in Addiction. 30. Wagenaar AC, Tobler AL, and Komro KA (2010) systematically review the effects of alcohol tax price policies on morbidity and mortality, as reported in the American Journal of Public Health. 31. Warner KE (2000) debunks myths and realities surrounding the economics of tobacco in Tobacco Control. 32. Willis J (2003) explores the uncertain boundaries of criminal enterprise in modern Kenya in the context of new-generation drinking, as published in African Affairs. 33. Wittwer G and Anderson K (2002) analyze the impact of the GST and wine tax reform on Australia’s wine industry using a CGE analysis, as reported in Australian Economic Papers. 34. World Health Organization (2002) publishes the World Health Report 2002, focusing on reducing risks and promoting healthy life, in Geneva. 35. World Health Organization (2010a) outlines a global strategy to reduce the harmful use of alcohol, published in Geneva. 36. World Health Organization (2010b) releases a technical manual on tobacco tax administration, published in Geneva. 37. World Health Organization (2011) and (2012) report on the outcomes of high-level meetings and conferences on non-communicable diseases and healthy lifestyles, published in Geneva. 38. World Health Organization (2014) publishes the Global Status Report on Alcohol and Health 2014, providing comprehensive data on alcohol consumption and its health impacts. 39. Zhang P, Yurekli A, and de Beyer J (2002) evaluate the impact of tobacco control policies on employment, as part of the World Bank Economics of Tobacco Toolkit, Tool 5, published in Washington, DC. 40. Ziegler D (2006) examines how international trade agreements challenge tobacco and alcohol control policies in Drug and Alcohol Review. 41. Ziegler D (2009) provides a preliminary assessment of the alcohol industry and trade agreements in Addiction. 42. The WHO Global Strategy emphasizes that consumers, including heavy drinkers and young people, are sensitive to changes in alcohol prices. Pricing policies can effectively reduce underage drinking, prevent progression to heavy drinking, and influence consumer preferences. Increasing the price of alcoholic beverages is one of the most effective interventions to reduce harmful alcohol use. The success of price-related policies depends on an efficient taxation system with adequate tax collection and enforcement.
